interest: For legal and diplomatic historians, this file provides a detailed case study in how international reciprocity functioned in practice between two distinct legal systems, especially navigating the decentralized nature of U.S. state bar admissions versus a centralized Japanese national statute. It documents the precarious position of Western professionals in pre-World War II Japan as the Japanese government tightened statutory controls over foreign practitioners amid growing nationalist consolidation. Additionally, the collection offers valuable historical context on figures such as William J. Sebald, who was practicing law in Kobe during this period before rising to prominent postwar diplomatic roles, including serving as the chief diplomatic adviser to General Douglas MacArthur during the Allied Occupation of Japan.
overview: This file covers diplomatic, legal, and administrative correspondence between November 1935 and October 1938 concerning the United States State Department's efforts to safeguard the professional practice rights of American attorneys residing in Japan—specifically William B. Spencer in Yokohama, William J. Sebald in Kobe, and C. C. Smith in Tokyo. Under Japan's Lawyers' Law of 1933 (Law No. 53), which took effect in April 1936, the practice of law was restricted strictly to Japanese subjects unless foreign reciprocity could be certified. In response, State Department officials, led by Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth, liaised with local bar and judicial authorities in the District of Columbia and Maryland to assemble authenticated chains of certificates demonstrating that Japanese nationals in those jurisdictions were permitted to advise on foreign and Japanese law without formal bar admission. These credentials and urgent instructions were dispatched to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew at the American Embassy in Tokyo for submission to the Japanese Ministry of Justice, alongside an incidental archival fragment concerning Japanese policy toward Chiang Kai-shek and China.
